1	# Market & audience
2	
3	The scale of the Edinburgh Fringe and the audience behaviour EdFringeNow is built
4	for. Two decisions live here, not one: the in-the-moment "what can I make right
5	now" (the home site, *Fringe Discover*) and the weeks-earlier "which shows, which
6	dates" (the planner at `/plan`). Compiled once, refined in place.
7	
8	## Scale
9	
10	### 2026 festival (running 7–31 August 2026)
11	
12	- **3,649 shows** across **258 venues**, **53,884 performances**, artists from
13	  **71 countries** — announced at the programme launch on 4 June 2026.
14	- Genre split at launch: **1,401 comedy**, **1,025 theatre**, **168 musicals and
15	  opera**.
16	- Smaller than 2025 on both counts (3,893 shows / 301 venues), and still two
17	  orders of magnitude more than any one visitor can see.
18	
19	### 2025 festival (latest full ticket data)
20	
21	- **3,893 shows** across **301 venues**, **53,942 performances**, artists from
22	  **62 countries**.
23	- **~2.6 million tickets** issued (2,604,404) — roughly flat on 2024, still below
24	  the 2019 pre-pandemic peak of about 3 million.
25	- **edfringe.com took over 3 million visits and 37 million page views**, and
26	  ~4,300 professional reviews were uploaded to the site to help audiences choose.
27	
28	*(2025's ticket figures stay on this page because they remain the newest
29	issued-ticket data — the Fringe Society publishes each year's ticket and audience
30	data after the festival closes, so 2026's cannot land before late August 2026.)*
31	
32	This scale is the product premise: the official programme is a catalogue that
33	rewards planning ahead and overwhelms the person deciding in the moment.
34	
35	## The overwhelm / decision problem
36	
37	Fringe Society audience data puts numbers on it:
38	
39	- **37% of audiences struggled to pick a show** to go and see.
40	- **Two thirds of ticket buyers bought only one ticket** — for most of the
41	  audience the Fringe is a single decision, not a curated run of shows.
42	- **78% came to the Fringe to see something they wouldn't go and see otherwise** —
43	  the appetite is for discovery, not for a known quantity.
44	
45	The standard advice around that, consistent across guides and relevant to both
46	surfaces:
47	
48	- With more than 3,800 shows, choosing "can feel like a daunting task"; the
49	  advice is to lean on filters, star ratings and reviews, and to **embrace
50	  serendipity** — the show you'd never have booked is often the one people still
51	  talk about.
52	- **Leave travel time.** Edinburgh is compact but August streets are not; guides
53	  repeat that venues which look close together are not close in August — the
54	  reachability constraint Fringe Discover makes first-class rather than an
55	  afterthought.
56	- **Two to three shows a day** is the pace commonly advised as comfortable —
57	  leaving room to eat, walk, and stand still.
58	- **Don't fill the day.** Fringe CEO Tony Lankester's "rule of thirds" — about a
59	  third of the time pre-planned, the rest left open — alongside reporting that
60	  visitors who combined structured planning with open time were more satisfied
61	  than those who over-scheduled.
62	
63	That last point is load-bearing here: the gaps a planner deliberately leaves are
64	exactly the gaps the live surface exists to fill.
65	
66	## Two crowds, not one
67	
68	This page previously described a single audience (the in-the-moment one) because
69	it was seeded from the *Fringe Discover* brief. The repo now ships two front
70	ends — the mobile-first home site and the desktop-first planner at `/plan` — and
71	they serve different people, or the same people in different states.
72	
73	### A. Live, in-festival — "what can I make right now"
74	
75	- **On the ground, deciding for the next hour or two.** Location, travel mode and
76	  the next commitment are the constraints; the catalogue is noise.
77	- **A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh** — locals have no trip to plan and
78	  no accommodation to book, and decide close to the moment by construction.
79	- **Same-day supply is a real channel, and an in-person one.** The Half Price Hut
80	  sells same-day (and next-morning) tickets from the Fringe Box Office only — not
81	  online, not in the app — opening 12 August in 2026, 10:00–18:00 daily.
82	- **Walk-up availability is not constant across the run.** Guides report walk-ups
83	  are easy in the opening week and that by weeks two and three popular shows —
84	  comedy headliners especially — sell out days in advance. The live surface's
85	  usefulness therefore moves with the calendar as well as the hour.
86	- **How the decision is actually made in the street is undocumented.** Posters,
87	  Royal Mile flyering, star ratings and word of mouth clearly drive a large share
88	  of it, but practitioners writing about Fringe marketing state plainly that
89	  nobody knows what works — there is no measured breakdown of in-the-moment
90	  discovery channels to cite.
91	
92	### B. Trip planners optimising around favourite shows
93	
94	- **Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh** — they choose dates,
95	  book beds and travel, and assemble a show list long before August.
96	- **Audiences now engage months ahead.** Reporting on how the Fringe audience has
97	  changed describes a 2026 audience that follows artists online, votes in polls
98	  and treats the festival as a live-entertainment marketplace well before August —
99	  a marked shift from the "turn up and grab a flyer" Fringe of a decade ago.
100	- **Accommodation binds *which dates* a trip can happen**, not as a footnote:
101	  coverage of the festival's accommodation crisis reports over half of people
102	  hoping to attend could not find an affordable place to stay within a 90-minute
103	  commute. Dates get chosen against beds as much as against shows — something the
104	  planner's "pick my best dates" currently ignores.
105	- **The favourites list is the planner's raw material, and it lives elsewhere.**
106	  Shows are favourited on edfringe.com and saved in the official app's *My
107	  Planner* (which syncs to a personal calendar). Getting that list *out* as a CSV
108	  is served by a third-party Chrome extension ("EdFringe Favourites to CSV",
109	  updated per festival year); no native edfringe.com CSV export is documented.
110	  The planner's front door depends on an export path we do not own.
111	- **The programme launch is the season's starting gun.** The 2026 programme went
112	  live on 4 June 2026, with shows revealed in batches from 11 February — so
113	  planning demand exists for months before any live demand can.
114	
115	### The same person, at different hours
116	
117	These are not necessarily two populations. The rule-of-thirds advice describes one
118	visitor who pre-plans part of a day and leaves the rest open; the planner serves
119	that first third and the live surface the other two. What differs is not identity
120	but **state** — horizon, device, inputs, and what "correct" even means. Those
121	differences are worked through on their own page:
122	[audience-divergence/](../audience-divergence/README.md). Nothing on this page
123	should be read as implying one merged requirement set.
124	
125	## Audience segments (product-brief hypotheses)
126	
127	From the product brief (`docs/product-spec.md`, an internal hypothesis not yet
128	externally validated): visitors mid-festival on foot without a fixed plan; people
129	with a _gap_ between commitments; locals and tourists intimidated by the
130	programme's size. Decisive in the moment rather than researchers, with an
131	emotional target of "delight + relief."
132	
133	Those segments describe crowd **A** only — the brief predates `/plan`, and no
134	equivalent written segmentation exists for the trip-planning crowd. The partial
135	external evidence for crowd B is the block above (two thirds non-resident,
136	months-ahead engagement, accommodation-first date choice); a validated
137	segmentation for either crowd remains an open question.
138	
139	## Sources
140	
141	- [The 2026 Edinburgh Festival Fringe programme is now live (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/mixitup-with-the-2026-edinburgh-festival-fringe-programme/)
142	- [Edinburgh Festival Fringe 2026 programme launched with 3,649 shows from 71 countries (Theatre Weekly)](https://theatreweekly.com/edinburgh-festival-fringe-2026-programme-launched-with-3649-shows-from-71-countries/)
143	- [Key dates for your diary in the lead-up to Fringe 2026 (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/key-dates-for-your-diary-in-the-lead-up-to-fringe-2026/)
144	- [Edinburgh Festival Fringe issues over 2.6 million tickets across 3,893 shows (BroadwayWorld)](https://www.broadwayworld.com/article/Edinburgh-Festival-Fringe-Issues-Over-26-Million-Tickets-Across-3893-Shows-20250826)
145	- [Fringe Society releases 2025 ticket and audience data (WhatsOnStage)](https://www.whatsonstage.com/news/edinburgh-festival-fringe-society-releases-ticket-and-audience-data-as-2025-event-concludes_1692055/)
146	- [We've published our review of the year 2025 (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/weve-published-our-review-of-the-year-2025/)
147	- [An exciting and energising Edinburgh Festival Fringe 2025 comes to a close (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/an-exciting-and-energising-edinburgh-festival-fringe-2025-comes-to-a-close/)
148	- [How to use your audience data with a purpose: the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (Thrive)](https://wewillthrive.co.uk/resources/case-studies/how-to-use-your-audience-data-with-a-purpose-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/)
149	- [Fringe 2026 — How the Audience Has Changed (The Edinburgh Reporter)](https://theedinburghreporter.co.uk/2026/05/fringe-2026-how-the-audience-has-changed/)
150	- [Edinburgh Fringe 2026: First-Timer's Planning Guide (Discover Edinburgh Fringe)](https://discoveredinburghfringe.com/en/blog/edinburgh-fringe-2026-first-timers-planning-guide)
151	- [Ten tips for Fringe first-timers in 2026 (Edinburgh Festival City)](https://www.edinburghfestivalcity.com/inspiration/128-five-tips-for-fringe-first-timers)
152	- [Half Price Hut (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/tickets/half-price-hut)
153	- [Edinburgh Festival Fringe Box Office (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/experience/plan-your-visit/fringe-box-office/)
154	- [Late night transport and 'live dashboard' could solve Edinburgh's festival accommodation crisis (The Scotsman)](https://www.scotsman.com/arts-and-culture/late-night-transport-and-live-dashboard-could-solve-edinburghs-festival-accommodation-crisis-5239090)
155	- [EdFringe Favourites to CSV (Chrome Web Store)](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/edfringe-favourites-to-cs/ebbiecdkhoclnlgfibfhhnpfhmmgdbcc)
156	- [Fringe app — Edinburgh Festival Fringe](https://www.edfringe.com/experience/plan-your-visit/fringe-app/)
157	- [Marketing at the Fringe: Everyone Has Theories. No One Has Data. (Danielle Solof)](https://www.daniellesolof.com/home/2025/10/23/marketing-at-the-fringe-everyone-has-theories-no-one-has-data)
158	- [3,000 Shows, So Little Time! How to Choose (Playbill)](https://playbill.com/article/3-000-shows-so-little-time-how-to-pick-what-to-see-at-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe)
159	- [How to choose which shows to see at the Fringe (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/how-to-choose-which-shows-to-see-at-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/)
160	
161	## Open questions
162	
163	- **Sizing the two crowds.** "A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh" is the
164	  only hard split found; there is still no cited figure for spontaneous /
165	  gap-filling versus pre-planned attendance, nor for how many of the two thirds
166	  from outside Edinburgh are day-trippers (no accommodation decision) versus
167	  multi-night stays (the planner's real crowd).
168	- **How the in-the-moment decision is really made.** Still no measured breakdown
169	  of in-street discovery channels — the honest current answer is that nobody has
170	  the data. A small first-party observation (even n=20 on the Royal Mile) would
171	  beat the citation vacuum.
172	- **When planning happens.** No cited series for advance-versus-same-day
173	  purchasing, or for how sales pace across the run. This decides whether the
174	  planner is a June–July product or an all-August one.
175	- **Does the favourites list have a native export?** The third-party CSV
176	  extension exists; whether edfringe.com itself offers an export — and how many
177	  people ever produce one — is unconfirmed, and the planner's intake depends on
178	  it.
179	- **Accommodation as a planning input.** No authoritative price/availability
180	  series found (guide-site figures only). If beds constrain dates more than shows
181	  do, "pick my best dates" optimises the wrong variable — worth evidence before
182	  acting on it.
183	- Refresh the ticket/audience figures once the 2026 festival's data is published.
184

190	  cited.
191	- **2026-07-28** — took the `/plan` surface into account and split the page from
192	  one audience into two crowds (live in-festival; trip planners optimising around
193	  favourites). Added 2026 scale figures (3,649 shows / 258 venues / 53,884
194	  performances / 71 countries, 7–31 Aug) alongside the retained 2025 ticket data;

198	  picture, the non-resident share, the accommodation constraint on date choice,
199	  and the third-party favourites-CSV dependency. Recorded that the product
200	  brief's segments cover crowd A only. Open questions rewritten in both
201	  directions. Requirements implication (two requirement tracks, not one) left for
202	  human review — see the audience-divergence page.

4	(the mobile-first home site, "what can I make right now") and the planner at
5	`/plan` (desktop-first, "which of my favourites can I catch, on which dates").

7	requirements** — where they pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the
8	narrow spine they genuinely share.
9	
10	It is research, not requirements: nothing here is a decision. The requirements
11	implication (two tracks rather than one) is for a human to promote into
12	`product-wiki/product-requirements/`.
13	
14	## The two crowds in a line each
15	
16	- **Live, in-festival.** On the ground in Edinburgh during 7–31 August, deciding
17	  for the next hour or two. A third of the Fringe audience lives in Edinburgh and
18	  has no trip to plan at all; most ticket buyers buy a single ticket.
19	- **Trip planners.** Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh,
20	  choose dates and beds, and assemble a favourites list months before August —
21	  the 2026 programme launched on 4 June, and audiences now engage with the
22	  festival long before it starts.
23	
24	They may be the same person in different states — the Fringe CEO's "rule of
25	thirds" describes one visitor pre-planning about a third of their time and
26	leaving the rest open. That does not make it one requirement set; it makes the
27	handover between the two surfaces a design problem in its own right.
28	
29	## Where they diverge
30	
31	| Axis | Live surface | Planner |
32	|---|---|---|
33	| **Horizon** | the next 1–2 hours | a stay chosen weeks out, then re-tuned |
34	| **Origin** | device location, "here, now" | no useful location; an accommodation base at best |
35	| **Taste input** | zero-effort defaults, genre chips, free/paid | an explicit favourites list built elsewhere, at high effort |
36	| **Correctness** | is this *still* catchable — a live fact | will this *be* catchable — a forecast that decays |
37	| **Objective** | one good, reachable option now | a whole trip's worth, and which dates make it possible |
38	| **Cost of error** | a wasted walk, a late entrance | non-refundable tickets, travel and beds booked around a wrong plan |
39	| **Device & context** | phone, outdoors, one hand, sunlight, patchy signal | desktop, indoors, deliberate, wide canvas |
40	| **Time to value** | seconds; typing is failure | minutes of deliberate work is acceptable |
41	| **State** | stateless — the answer expires with the hour | persistent — favourites, window, itinerary, exports (CSV/ICS) |
42	| **Season** | only 7–31 August, and value shifts across the run | February–July, peaking after each programme drop |
43	| **Success** | "I chose something and I made it" | "N of my favourites got caught, and the days were liveable" |
44	
45	## Requirements that actively conflict
46	
47	These are the places where satisfying one crowd well makes the other worse.
48	Naming them is the point of this page.
49	
50	1. **Pack the day vs leave the day open.** The planner's allocator is an
51	   earliest-finish-first greedy — it maximises the number of shows placed. The
52	   audience evidence points the other way: two to three shows a day is the pace
53	   commonly advised, visitors who combined structured planning with open time
54	   reported higher satisfaction than over-schedulers, and the rule of thirds asks
55	   for roughly a third of the time planned. A planner that fills the day
56	   optimally also destroys the gaps the live surface serves. The two surfaces can
57	   be jointly optimal only if the planner's objective is *not* "maximum shows".
58	2. **Live truth vs planning truth, from one catalogue.** Both surfaces read the
59	   same `data/normalized/shows.json`. For the live surface, sold-out /
60	   started-already is a *fact* and staleness is the core failure mode. For the
61	   planner, the same field is a *forecast* about a date weeks away, which decays
62	   in the opposite direction (shows sell out as August approaches; walk-ups are
63	   easy in week one and scarce in weeks two and three). Identical data, two
64	   incompatible honesty obligations — the planner arguably must show "may sell
65	   out before you book" where the live surface must show "gone".
66	3. **Zero input vs high-effort input.** The brief's live target is "a brand-new
67	   user with zero taps already sees useful results". The planner's front door is
68	   a CSV export the user produces on another site — and, as far as the research
69	   shows, via a third-party browser extension. One surface's core virtue is
70	   asking nothing; the other's is asking for something quite hard to obtain.
71	4. **Personalisation model.** Live personalisation is coarse taste (ten festival
72	   genres, free/paid) applied to whatever is reachable. Planner personalisation
73	   is an explicit, already-curated favourites set — a different data model, a
74	   different privacy posture (the planner keeps parsed favourites in
75	   `localStorage` for three days; the live surface keeps nothing), and different
76	   recommendation logic. Merging them into "one personalisation system" would
77	   serve neither.
78	5. **What "optimise" even means.** Live: maximise the chance the user goes and
79	   enjoys one show inside a slack budget. Planner: maximise favourites caught
80	   across a window — and, upstream of that, choose the window. The planner's
81	   *most valuable* question ("when should I come?") has no live analogue at all,
82	   and no profiled competitor answers it.
83	6. **Which constraints are even visible.** The live surface's binding constraint
84	   is travel time to the next commitment. The planner's real binding constraint
85	   may not be shows at all: over half of would-be attendees reportedly could not
86	   find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute, so dates are chosen
87	   against beds. `/plan`'s "pick my best dates" scores windows purely on show
88	   catchability — optimising a variable the user may not be free to move.
89	7. **Failure of the map.** Live, a map answers "where is that relative to me".
90	   In the planner, there is no "me" — the map's job becomes clustering and
91	   walkability across a day, which is a different visualisation with different
92	   requirements (and the reason the planner's schedule draws travel legs rather
93	   than a map).
94	
95	## What the two genuinely share
96	
97	Small, and worth keeping small deliberately:
98	
99	- **One catalogue and one venue geometry** — the scraped `shows.json` /
100	  `venues.json`, already shared, plus the haversine + per-mode travel model in
101	  `plan/lib/travel.js` and the `UK_BOUNDS` helper both front ends import.
102	- **Honesty about data gaps** — no ticket prices beyond free/paid, no live seat

109	  plan says you're free until 19:00"), and that connection is the one place where
110	  a *shared* requirement would be justified.

129	  on how many planner users are also in Edinburgh mid-festival. If the overlap is

# Audience divergence — the live crowd vs the trip planners

EdFringeNow now points at two decisions with two front ends: *Fringe Discover*
(the mobile-first home site, "what can I make right now") and the planner at
`/plan` (desktop-first, "which of my favourites can I catch, on which dates").
This page exists to hold the evidence that **the two do not reduce to one set of
requirements** — where they pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the
narrow spine they genuinely share.

It is research, not requirements: nothing here is a decision. The requirements
implication (two tracks rather than one) is for a human to promote into
`product-wiki/product-requirements/`.

## The two crowds in a line each

- **Live, in-festival.** On the ground in Edinburgh during 7–31 August, deciding
  for the next hour or two. A third of the Fringe audience lives in Edinburgh and
  has no trip to plan at all; most ticket buyers buy a single ticket.
- **Trip planners.** Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh,
  choose dates and beds, and assemble a favourites list months before August —
  the 2026 programme launched on 4 June, and audiences now engage with the
  festival long before it starts.

They may be the same person in different states — the Fringe CEO's "rule of
thirds" describes one visitor pre-planning about a third of their time and
leaving the rest open. That does not make it one requirement set; it makes the
handover between the two surfaces a design problem in its own right.

## Where they diverge

| Axis | Live surface | Planner |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizon** | the next 1–2 hours | a stay chosen weeks out, then re-tuned |
| **Origin** | device location, "here, now" | no useful location; an accommodation base at best |
| **Taste input** | zero-effort defaults, genre chips, free/paid | an explicit favourites list built elsewhere, at high effort |
| **Correctness** | is this *still* catchable — a live fact | will this *be* catchable — a forecast that decays |
| **Objective** | one good, reachable option now | a whole trip's worth, and which dates make it possible |
| **Cost of error** | a wasted walk, a late entrance | non-refundable tickets, travel and beds booked around a wrong plan |
| **Device & context** | phone, outdoors, one hand, sunlight, patchy signal | desktop, indoors, deliberate, wide canvas |
| **Time to value** | seconds; typing is failure | minutes of deliberate work is acceptable |
| **State** | stateless — the answer expires with the hour | persistent — favourites, window, itinerary, exports (CSV/ICS) |
| **Season** | only 7–31 August, and value shifts across the run | February–July, peaking after each programme drop |
| **Success** | "I chose something and I made it" | "N of my favourites got caught, and the days were liveable" |

## Requirements that actively conflict

These are the places where satisfying one crowd well makes the other worse.
Naming them is the point of this page.

1. **Pack the day vs leave the day open.** The planner's allocator is an
   earliest-finish-first greedy — it maximises the number of shows placed. The
   audience evidence points the other way: two to three shows a day is the pace
   commonly advised, visitors who combined structured planning with open time
   reported higher satisfaction than over-schedulers, and the rule of thirds asks
   for roughly a third of the time planned. A planner that fills the day
   optimally also destroys the gaps the live surface serves. The two surfaces can
   be jointly optimal only if the planner's objective is *not* "maximum shows".
2. **Live truth vs planning truth, from one catalogue.** Both surfaces read the
   same `data/normalized/shows.json`. For the live surface, sold-out /
   started-already is a *fact* and staleness is the core failure mode. For the
   planner, the same field is a *forecast* about a date weeks away, which decays
   in the opposite direction (shows sell out as August approaches; walk-ups are
   easy in week one and scarce in weeks two and three). Identical data, two
   incompatible honesty obligations — the planner arguably must show "may sell
   out before you book" where the live surface must show "gone".
3. **Zero input vs high-effort input.** The brief's live target is "a brand-new
   user with zero taps already sees useful results". The planner's front door is
   a CSV export the user produces on another site — and, as far as the research
   shows, via a third-party browser extension. One surface's core virtue is
   asking nothing; the other's is asking for something quite hard to obtain.
4. **Personalisation model.** Live personalisation is coarse taste (ten festival
   genres, free/paid) applied to whatever is reachable. Planner personalisation
   is an explicit, already-curated favourites set — a different data model, a
   different privacy posture (the planner keeps parsed favourites in
   `localStorage` for three days; the live surface keeps nothing), and different
   recommendation logic. Merging them into "one personalisation system" would
   serve neither.
5. **What "optimise" even means.** Live: maximise the chance the user goes and
   enjoys one show inside a slack budget. Planner: maximise favourites caught
   across a window — and, upstream of that, choose the window. The planner's
   *most valuable* question ("when should I come?") has no live analogue at all,
   and no profiled competitor answers it.
6. **Which constraints are even visible.** The live surface's binding constraint
   is travel time to the next commitment. The planner's real binding constraint
   may not be shows at all: over half of would-be attendees reportedly could not
   find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute, so dates are chosen
   against beds. `/plan`'s "pick my best dates" scores windows purely on show
   catchability — optimising a variable the user may not be free to move.
7. **Failure of the map.** Live, a map answers "where is that relative to me".
   In the planner, there is no "me" — the map's job becomes clustering and
   walkability across a day, which is a different visualisation with different
   requirements (and the reason the planner's schedule draws travel legs rather
   than a map).

## What the two genuinely share

Small, and worth keeping small deliberately:

- **One catalogue and one venue geometry** — the scraped `shows.json` /
  `venues.json`, already shared, plus the haversine + per-mode travel model in
  `plan/lib/travel.js` and the `UK_BOUNDS` helper both front ends import.
- **Honesty about data gaps** — no ticket prices beyond free/paid, no live seat
  counts beyond a sold-out flag. Neither surface may imply data we don't have.
- **The same emotional promise** — the overwhelm lifting. 37% of audiences
  reported struggling to pick a show; both surfaces exist to answer that, at
  different distances from the decision.
- **A handover, in one direction.** The planner's deliberate gaps are the live
  surface's demand. Nothing today connects them (no shared favourites, no "your
  plan says you're free until 19:00"), and that connection is the one place where
  a *shared* requirement would be justified.

## Sources

- [How to use your audience data with a purpose: the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (Thrive)](https://wewillthrive.co.uk/resources/case-studies/how-to-use-your-audience-data-with-a-purpose-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/) — a third of the audience lives in Edinburgh; two thirds of ticket buyers bought one ticket; 37% struggled to pick a show.

- [Late night transport and 'live dashboard' could solve Edinburgh's festival accommodation crisis (The Scotsman)](https://www.scotsman.com/arts-and-culture/late-night-transport-and-live-dashboard-could-solve-edinburghs-festival-accommodation-crisis-5239090) — over half unable to find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute.
- [The 2026 Edinburgh Festival Fringe programme is now live (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/mixitup-with-the-2026-edinburgh-festival-fringe-programme/) — 4 June 2026 launch; 7–31 August dates.
- [EdFringe Favourites to CSV (Chrome Web Store)](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/edfringe-favourites-to-cs/ebbiecdkhoclnlgfibfhhnpfhmmgdbcc) — the third-party export path the planner's intake depends on.

  is small, the two products should probably diverge further, not converge.

## Key insights

- **3,649 shows across 258 venues in 2026** — two orders of magnitude more than
  any one visitor can see, which is why a catalogue is the wrong shape for the
  person deciding now.
- **37% of audiences struggle to pick a show, and two thirds of ticket buyers buy
  exactly one ticket** — for most people the Fringe is a single hard decision,
  not a curated run of shows.
- **78% come to see something they wouldn't otherwise go and see** — the appetite
  is discovery, so the answer is not filtering harder but making a good option
  reachable.
- **There are two crowds, not one.** A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh
  and decides by the hour; two thirds travel in and choose dates, beds and a
  favourites list months ahead.
- **The advice everyone repeats is "don't fill the day"** — two to three shows,
  about a third of the time planned (the Fringe CEO's rule of thirds). The gaps a
  planner leaves are exactly what the live surface exists to fill.
- **Dates may be chosen against beds, not shows** — over half of would-be
  attendees reportedly could not find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute
  commute, a constraint `/plan`'s date scoring ignores.
- **Nobody has data on how the in-street decision is actually made**, and the
  product brief's audience segments cover the live crowd only — both remain
  unvalidated.

## Key insights

- **The two surfaces do not reduce to one requirement set** — that is this page's

  human's call.
- **Their objectives conflict outright.** The planner's greedy allocator
  maximises shows placed; the audience evidence says a good day is two or three
  shows with room left — the very gaps the live surface serves.
- **One catalogue, two incompatible honesty obligations.** Sold-out is a live
  *fact* for the live surface and a decaying *forecast* for a plan made in June;
  the same field cannot be presented the same way on both.
- **Zero input versus high-effort input.** The live surface's core virtue is
  asking nothing; the planner's front door is a favourites CSV the user extracts
  on another site, via a third-party browser extension.
- **"When should I come?" has no live analogue** — and no profiled competitor
  answers it. It is the planner's most valuable question and its least shared
  one.
- **What the two genuinely share is small**: one catalogue and venue geometry,
  the travel model, honesty about missing data, and the same emotional promise of
  lifting the overwhelm.
- **The one place a shared requirement is justified is the handover** — plan →
  live, "your plan says you're free until 19:00" — and nothing today connects
  them.

## Key insights

- **The two surfaces do not reduce to one requirement set** — that is this page's
  finding. It is evidence, not a decision: promoting it into requirements is a
  human's call.
- **Their objectives conflict outright.** The planner's greedy allocator
  maximises shows placed; the audience evidence says a good day is two or three
  shows with room left — the very gaps the live surface serves.
- **One catalogue, two incompatible honesty obligations.** Sold-out is a live
  *fact* for the live surface and a decaying *forecast* for a plan made in June;
  the same field cannot be presented the same way on both.
- **Zero input versus high-effort input.** The live surface's core virtue is
  asking nothing; the planner's front door is a favourites CSV the user extracts
  on another site, via a third-party browser extension.
- **"When should I come?" has no live analogue** — and no profiled competitor
  answers it. It is the planner's most valuable question and its least shared
  one.
- **What the two genuinely share is small**: one catalogue and venue geometry,
  the travel model, honesty about missing data, and the same emotional promise of
  lifting the overwhelm.
- **The one place a shared requirement is justified is the handover** — plan →
  live, "your plan says you're free until 19:00" — and nothing today connects
  them.

input.body:
A compiled research page is only useful if a human can get its findings without reading it end to end. Every `product-wiki/` page now **opens with `## Key insights`** — a short bulleted list of what the research actually found, ahead of every other section. The body stays the research record; the header is where a reader decides whether they need it.

## The contract, and who enforces which half

Split along the pack's existing ownership line, so nothing is double-reported:

- **`product-wiki-page-sections`** gains `Key insights` as a fourth required section — a missing header is reported exactly once, in the same place every other missing section is.
- **`product-wiki-key-insights`** (new, blocking) owns the header's *shape*: it leads every other section, it is bullets only, it carries at least one and at most seven, and no bullet runs past 300 characters. A bullet's indented continuation lines count as part of it, so hard-wrapping is free and a wrapped essay bullet can't hide.

*Which* insights lead — and keeping them true as research moves — is judgment, so it lives in prose, not in a check:

- **RULES.md**: the header carries conclusions (the numbers, the competitor that already ships this, the thing that turned out not to be true), never a table of contents; and it is a **current view, not a log** — a pass that changes the page's top-line understanding rewrites it, a pass that doesn't leaves it alone.
- **The wiki-growth worker** gains a reconcile step in its method, plus a must-never-do: leaving a header asserting what the body it heads no longer says.

## Tested against real wikis, not just fixtures

EdFringeNow's three research wikis were the testing ground (headers landed there as [a separate PR](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pulls)).

- Before: `page-sections` fires once per page naming the missing header; `key-insights` stays silent (correctly — the missing heading isn't its finding).
- After: all four page checks clean.
- Calibration: real distilled insight bullets came out **140–230 characters**, so the 300 cap has genuine headroom while still catching a paragraph pasted into the header. Seven bullets was a comfortable fit for pages this dense, not a squeeze.

Six new unit tests; four of the six fail if the check's `run` is neutered (the other two are clean-passes tests, correctly insensitive). Full suite 897/897, conformance sweep 0 blocking.

## Fleet propagation

No migration record. Existing members converge through the nightly baselining: a missing header is precisely the "blocking finding that needs judgment" its worker resolves on the maintenance PR. A record also couldn't carry honest telemetry here — wiki pages are discovered *structurally*, which `legacyPresent`'s path-reader cannot enumerate, so it would never auto-retire.

One dated growth-log entry per page, recording that the change is the header and nothing else.

The new canon checks were run against this tree directly. Before: `product-wiki-page-sections` fired once per page for the missing header. # product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki

This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape,
growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are
**check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates
them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc
(`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`).

- **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a
  few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the
  competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true —
  enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
  and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"),
  not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
- **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's
  most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded
  insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below),
  and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's
  top-line understanding, the header doesn't move.
- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  build on.
- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.

# product-wiki pack

The self-growing product research wiki standard: a repo keeps its
market/user/competitor research as agent-maintained wikis under `product-wiki/`
(Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern — compile findings once, refine in place, cite
everything), walled off from the code so nothing can silently depend on
unreviewed research, with one human-reviewed crossing point. Declared by the
project (fingerprint: `product-wiki/product-requirements/README.md` — the sink is
the standard's one structural constant). Takes **no config**: the layout is the
standard.

## The standard

- `product-wiki/` at the repo root. Two reserved children with fixed meaning:
  **`product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the
  wikis into product requirements, the **only** `product-wiki/` content the rest of
  the repo may reference, never auto-grown — and **`product-wiki/sample-data/`** —
  small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (never test fixtures).
- **Everything else under `product-wiki/` is wiki space** — any names, any nesting.
  A wiki page is a `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under `product-wiki/` outside the two
  reserved subtrees. The folder is the classifier; there is no wikis manifest
  to drift, and a renamed wiki folder is still a wiki folder — still checked,
  still barred.
- Every wiki page **opens with `## Key insights`** — up to seven short bullets
  carrying what the research found, ahead of every other section. The body is
  the research record; the header is what makes it readable, so a human who
  reads only the header understands what was researched and what came of it.
- Every wiki page also carries `## Sources` (every source bullet carrying its
  real URL), `## Growth log` (dated bullets, newest change appended per pass),
  and `## Open questions` (the research backlog the growth passes work from).
- Growth is scheduled research: the pack's weekly scheduled task
  ([tasks/wiki-growth/task.md](tasks/wiki-growth/task.md)) reads
  the wikis, researches what their own open questions flag, writes back cited,
  and delivers an unmerged PR. Most passes correctly change nothing.

## Rules

| Rule | Enforces (≤5 words) | How |
|---|---|---|
| `product-wiki-layout` | skeleton exists (index + sink) | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-page-sections` | pages carry the four sections | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-key-insights` | header leads, bulleted, succinct | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-growth-log` | log bullets dated, real dates | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-sources` | source bullets carry their URL | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-freshness` | stale wiki gets a nag | check, **advisory** |
| `product-wiki-isolation` | repo can't reference wiki space | check, blocking (fixed barrier) |
| sink is human-reviewed only | — | prose + worker must-never-do |
| cite / correct-with-note / no fabrication | — | prose + worker method |
| sample-data ≠ test fixtures | — | prose |
| unattended growth lands as unmerged PR | — | prose + worker delivery policy |

`product-wiki-key-insights` enforces the header's **shape** — it leads every other
section, it is bullets only, it carries at least one and at most seven, and no
bullet runs past 300 characters (a bullet's indented continuation lines count as
part of it, so hard-wrapping is free). *Which* insights lead, and keeping them
true as research moves, is judgment — that lives in RULES.md and the growth
worker, and no check can score it. The missing heading itself is
`product-wiki-page-sections`' finding, never double-reported.

`product-wiki-freshness` is advisory **by design**, not as a maturity stage: it
is time-driven (a repo goes stale with no change to its tree), and a
wall-clock-dependent finding must never block a Stop or fail CI. It fires per
page after 45 days without a growth-log entry — the in-repo observer for "the
unattended growth channel silently stopped firing". Silence it with
`rules: {"product-wiki-freshness": "off"}`.

## Scaffold template

```
product-wiki/
  README.md                        # index: what lives here, why it's walled off
  product-requirements/README.md   # the human-reviewed sink (required)
  <YourWiki>/README.md             # one folder per wiki — seeded like this:
```

```markdown
# <YourWiki>

What this wiki tracks, in a sentence or two.

## Key insights

- The first thing a reader needs to know, stated as the finding itself.
- ...up to seven; each one insight, a sentence or so, no citation clutter.

## <Your content sections>

## Sources

- [Title](https://real.url/)

## Open questions

- What should the next growth pass look into?

## Growth log

- **YYYY-MM-DD** — initial seed.
```

## Excusing a deliberate crossing (accept, not except)

`product-wiki-isolation` is a **fixed** barrier — its edges are pack code, so a
consumer cannot add the barriers pack's per-rule `except` entries to it. Each
crossing finding's own fix text says so and names the lever that works: a
top-level (or pack-entry) **accept**:

```json
"accept": [
  { "rule": "product-wiki-isolation", "path": "docs/inventory.md",
    "reason": "historical ledger — enumerates the wikis it catalogs" }
]
```

Matched by rule id + exact path (or a `dir/` prefix for a subtree); the reason
is mandatory. Unlike a barrier rule's own `except`, accepts are **not**
staleness-audited — prune one by hand when the crossing it excused is gone.

## Bootstrap ordering

Declaring the pack before scaffolding `product-wiki/` yields two `layout` findings
plus the barrier's fail-closed empty-glob finding — three blocking arrows all
pointing at the same two-file scaffold. That is deliberate: a declaration is a
statement of intent, unlike the barriers pack's unconfigured no-op (where
config absence means "nothing declared").

## Known gaps

- The barrier engine never scans `*.test.mjs`/test files as sources, so a test
  importing from wiki space is invisible to `product-wiki-isolation` — covered
  by prose (nothing a test asserts against belongs under `product-wiki/`), not
  fought in code.
- Accepts against `product-wiki-isolation` are pruned by hand (no staleness
  audit — see above).
- The weekly growth task rides the repo's own scheduler
  ([../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md](../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md));
  a repo without a `taskScheduler` anchor gets no unattended growth — the freshness
  advisory is the backstop that surfaces that, and the owner phrase "grow the
  product wiki" runs the same worker method in-session.

# product-wiki pack

The self-growing product research wiki standard: a repo keeps its
market/user/competitor research as agent-maintained wikis under `product-wiki/`
(Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern — compile findings once, refine in place, cite
everything), walled off from the code so nothing can silently depend on
unreviewed research, with one human-reviewed crossing point. Declared by the
project (fingerprint: `product-wiki/product-requirements/README.md` — the sink is
the standard's one structural constant). Takes **no config**: the layout is the
standard.

## The standard

- `product-wiki/` at the repo root. Two reserved children with fixed meaning:
  **`product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the
  wikis into product requirements, the **only** `product-wiki/` content the rest of
  the repo may reference, never auto-grown — and **`product-wiki/sample-data/`** —
  small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (never test fixtures).
- **Everything else under `product-wiki/` is wiki space** — any names, any nesting.
  A wiki page is a `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under `product-wiki/` outside the two
  reserved subtrees. The folder is the classifier; there is no wikis manifest
  to drift, and a renamed wiki folder is still a wiki folder — still checked,
  still barred.
- Every wiki page **opens with `## Key insights`** — up to seven bullets, one
  terse plain-words line each, carrying what the research found, ahead of every
  other section. The body is the research record; the header is what makes it
  readable, so a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
  and what came of it.
- Every wiki page also carries `## Sources` (every source bullet carrying its
  real URL), `## Growth log` (dated bullets, newest change appended per pass),
  and `## Open questions` (the research backlog the growth passes work from).
- Growth is scheduled research: the pack's weekly scheduled task
  ([tasks/wiki-growth/task.md](tasks/wiki-growth/task.md)) reads
  the wikis, researches what their own open questions flag, writes back cited,
  and delivers an unmerged PR. Most passes correctly change nothing.

## Rules

| Rule | Enforces (≤5 words) | How |
|---|---|---|
| `product-wiki-layout` | skeleton exists (index + sink) | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-page-sections` | pages carry the four sections | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-key-insights` | header leads, bulleted, succinct | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-growth-log` | log bullets dated, real dates | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-sources` | source bullets carry their URL | check, blocking |
| `product-wiki-freshness` | stale wiki gets a nag | check, **advisory** |
| `product-wiki-isolation` | repo can't reference wiki space | check, blocking (fixed barrier) |
| sink is human-reviewed only | — | prose + worker must-never-do |
| cite / correct-with-note / no fabrication | — | prose + worker method |
| sample-data ≠ test fixtures | — | prose |
| unattended growth lands as unmerged PR | — | prose + worker delivery policy |

`product-wiki-key-insights` enforces the header's **shape** — it leads every other
section, it is bullets only, it carries at least one and at most seven, and no
bullet runs past 300 characters (a bullet's indented continuation lines count as
part of it, so hard-wrapping is free). *Which* insights lead, and keeping them
true as research moves, is judgment — that lives in RULES.md and the growth
worker, and no check can score it. The missing heading itself is
`product-wiki-page-sections`' finding, never double-reported.

`product-wiki-freshness` is advisory **by design**, not as a maturity stage: it
is time-driven (a repo goes stale with no change to its tree), and a
wall-clock-dependent finding must never block a Stop or fail CI. It fires per
page after 45 days without a growth-log entry — the in-repo observer for "the
unattended growth channel silently stopped firing". Silence it with
`rules: {"product-wiki-freshness": "off"}`.

## Scaffold template

```
product-wiki/
  README.md                        # index: what lives here, why it's walled off
  product-requirements/README.md   # the human-reviewed sink (required)
  <YourWiki>/README.md             # one folder per wiki — seeded like this:
```

```markdown
# <YourWiki>

What this wiki tracks, in a sentence or two.

## Key insights

- The first thing a reader needs to know, stated as the finding itself.
- ...up to seven; each one insight, a sentence or so, no citation clutter.

## <Your content sections>

## Sources

- [Title](https://real.url/)

## Open questions

- What should the next growth pass look into?

## Growth log

- **YYYY-MM-DD** — initial seed.
```

## Excusing a deliberate crossing (accept, not except)

`product-wiki-isolation` is a **fixed** barrier — its edges are pack code, so a
consumer cannot add the barriers pack's per-rule `except` entries to it. Each
crossing finding's own fix text says so and names the lever that works: a
top-level (or pack-entry) **accept**:

```json
"accept": [
  { "rule": "product-wiki-isolation", "path": "docs/inventory.md",
    "reason": "historical ledger — enumerates the wikis it catalogs" }
]
```

Matched by rule id + exact path (or a `dir/` prefix for a subtree); the reason
is mandatory. Unlike a barrier rule's own `except`, accepts are **not**
staleness-audited — prune one by hand when the crossing it excused is gone.

## Bootstrap ordering

Declaring the pack before scaffolding `product-wiki/` yields two `layout` findings
plus the barrier's fail-closed empty-glob finding — three blocking arrows all
pointing at the same two-file scaffold. That is deliberate: a declaration is a
statement of intent, unlike the barriers pack's unconfigured no-op (where
config absence means "nothing declared").

## Known gaps

- The barrier engine never scans `*.test.mjs`/test files as sources, so a test
  importing from wiki space is invisible to `product-wiki-isolation` — covered
  by prose (nothing a test asserts against belongs under `product-wiki/`), not
  fought in code.
- Accepts against `product-wiki-isolation` are pruned by hand (no staleness
  audit — see above).
- The weekly growth task rides the repo's own scheduler
  ([../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md](../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md));
  a repo without a `taskScheduler` anchor gets no unattended growth — the freshness
  advisory is the backstop that surfaces that, and the owner phrase "grow the
  product wiki" runs the same worker method in-session.

`product-wiki/`, excluding the `product-wiki/product-requirements/` and `product-wiki/sample-data/` subtrees.

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: it may open a PR but never merges one and never pushes to
the default branch.

## Preflight

**Before researching**, search the repo for an open PR whose head branch matches `claude/product-wiki-growth/*`.
If one is open, do **not** stack a second round of unreviewed research on it — add one dated nudge comment on
that PR and stop.

This is the *only* guard against that stacking — nothing upstream covers it. The scheduler's at-most-one-open
guard is about **dispatch issues**, not pull requests: a completed run converges and closes its own dispatch
issue while leaving this task's PR open for the owner to review, so the next weekly slot sees an empty issue
family and dispatches normally. Expect to find an open growth PR whenever the last one hasn't been reviewed
yet; that is the ordinary case this preflight exists for, not an anomaly.

## Method

1. **Read every wiki page end to end** (`get_file_contents`), the `## Open questions` and `## Growth log`
   sections first-class. Never re-derive a claim that is already cited and current.
2. **Pick the one or two open questions** across the set most worth this run; also spot-check one or two
   existing citations for staleness (a dead link, a superseded stat). If the Context flagged a product-wiki
   change in the window, spot-check the pages it may have superseded.
3. **Research.** *Web mode* (WebSearch/WebFetch available): the open web. *Repo-derived mode* (web tools
   absent — do not fail, do not fake): citable repo-native signal only — new feature-request/extractor-request
   issues, merged PRs, issue/PR discussion carrying user-side signal — each citable to its own GitHub URL.
4. **Write into the relevant wiki page(s) only**, per the pack's RULES.md: cite every claim in that page's
   `## Sources`; correct a wrong or superseded claim with a note of why, never a silent deletion; touch
   `product-wiki/sample-data/` only when a new claim needs an illustrative example; **never write
   `product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — a finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note
   (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
5. **Reconcile the page's `## Key insights` header** with what the body now says. It leads the page, it is
   bullets only, and it is capped (seven bullets, ~300 characters each) — so a new insight that belongs at
   the top usually displaces a weaker one rather than being appended. Rewrite a bullet the run superseded
   (the correction and its *why* live in the body, not in the header); leave the header alone when the run
   changed nothing about the page's top-line understanding. **Never restate the header as a table of
   contents** — each bullet is a finding a reader can act on.
6. **One dated `## Growth log` entry per touched page** (`- **YYYY-MM-DD** — what changed`).
7. **Update `## Open questions` both directions** — remove what this run answered, add what its research
   surfaced.

## Stop condition

Neither mode yields citable material → stop. No commit, no log entry, no PR.

## Delivery

Branch `claude/product-wiki-growth/<date>` (unique branch per run), commits touching only `product-wiki/**`
minus `product-requirements/`, one **PR — never merged, never pushed to the default branch directly**.
Web-researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. PR body: the question(s)
researched, what changed where, the citations added, and the open questions left for the next run.

## Tracking

Standing issue found by exact title **"Claudinite tracker: Product Wiki Growth"** in the repo — found by
title, never by number, never opened/closed as state (open it if missing). One dated comment when a pass
**grew** (`grew (PR #N): <one line>`) or was **blocked** (`blocked: <why>` — the human-visible convergence for
a failed unattended run). Clean no-ops stay silent — the pack's freshness advisory is the prolonged-silence
observer.

`agent_model: opus` — open-web research plus curation is judgment-heavy, and the PR review gate is the last catch for
fabrication.

## What this worker must never do

Edit `product-wiki/product-requirements/`; edit anything outside `product-wiki/`; create new wiki folders
(automation refines existing pages — a human creates a wiki deliberately); write an uncited claim; delete a
claim without a superseded note; leave a `## Key insights` header asserting what the body it heads no longer
says; pad a growth log, a header, or a wiki page to look productive; merge or approve its own
PR; schedule anything (no cron, no `schedule:` workflow); touch the shared canon.

input.body:
A compiled research page is only useful if a human can get its findings without reading it end to end. Every `product-wiki/` page now **opens with `## Key insights`** — a few terse, plain-words lines carrying what the research found, ahead of every other section. The body stays the research record; the header is where a reader decides whether they need it.

Closes #543.

## The contract, and who enforces which half

Split along the pack's existing ownership line, so nothing is double-reported:

- **`product-wiki-page-sections`** gains `Key insights` as a fourth required section — a missing header is reported exactly once, in the same place every other missing section is.
- **`product-wiki-key-insights`** (new, blocking) owns the header's *shape*: it leads every other section, it is bullets only, it carries at least one and at most seven, and no bullet runs past **140 characters** — about one line. A bullet's indented continuation lines count as part of it, so hard-wrapping is free and a wrapped paragraph can't hide.

The tight cap is the point: a header earns its place only if it is faster to read than the page, and the failure mode in practice is a bullet that keeps qualifying itself. The qualifiers belong in the body.

*Which* insights lead, and how plainly they're worded, is judgment — so it lives in prose, not in a check:

- **RULES.md**: conclusions, never a table of contents. One short line per bullet in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would decode. Prefer what would *surprise* someone who knows the field. Judging obviousness is genuinely hard, so the error preference is stated outright: **when in doubt, keep the line** — a borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds, a long careful one costs them the header.
- **The header is a current view, not a log** — a pass that changes a page's top-line understanding rewrites it; a pass that doesn't leaves it alone. The wiki-growth worker gains that reconcile step, plus a must-never-do: leaving a header asserting what the body it heads no longer says.

## Tested against real wikis, not just fixtures

EdFringeNow's three research wikis were the testing ground; the headers land there as [EdFringeNow#146](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/146).

- Before: `page-sections` fires once per page naming the missing header; `key-insights` stays silent (correctly — the missing heading isn't its finding).
- After: all four page checks clean.
- Calibration: a first pass written to the old 300-char cap came out at 140–230 characters per bullet — readable, but paragraphs. Rewritten terse, the same seven findings per page fit in **66–93 characters**, so the 140 cap has real headroom for an honest line while cutting a paragraph off at the knees.

Six new unit tests; four of the six fail if the check's `run` is neutered (the other two are clean-pass tests, correctly insensitive). Full suite 897/897, conformance sweep 0 blocking.

## Fleet propagation

No migration record. Existing members converge through the nightly baselining: a missing header is precisely the "blocking finding that needs judgment" its worker resolves on the maintenance PR. A record also couldn't carry honest telemetry here — wiki pages are discovered *structurally*, which `legacyPresent`'s path-reader cannot enumerate, so it would never auto-retire.

2	
3	The self-growing product research wiki standard: a repo keeps its
4	market/user/competitor research as agent-maintained wikis under `product-wiki/`
5	(Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern — compile findings once, refine in place, cite
6	everything), walled off from the code so nothing can silently depend on
7	unreviewed research, with one human-reviewed crossing point. Declared by the
8	project (fingerprint: `product-wiki/product-requirements/README.md` — the sink is
9	the standard's one structural constant). Takes **no config**: the layout is the
10	standard.
11	
12	## The standard
13	
14	- `product-wiki/` at the repo root. Two reserved children with fixed meaning:
15	  **`product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the
16	  wikis into product requirements, the **only** `product-wiki/` content the rest of
17	  the repo may reference, never auto-grown — and **`product-wiki/sample-data/`** —
18	  small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (never test fixtures).
19	- **Everything else under `product-wiki/` is wiki space** — any names, any nesting.
20	  A wiki page is a `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under `product-wiki/` outside the two
21	  reserved subtrees. The folder is the classifier; there is no wikis manifest
22	  to drift, and a renamed wiki folder is still a wiki folder — still checked,
23	  still barred.
24	- Every wiki page carries `## Sources` (every source bullet carrying its real
25	  URL), `## Growth log` (dated bullets, newest change appended per pass), and
26	  `## Open questions` (the research backlog the growth passes work from).
27	- Growth is scheduled research: the pack's weekly `run_daily` task
28	  ([run_daily/wiki-growth.worker.md](run_daily/wiki-growth.worker.md)) reads
29	  the wikis, researches what their own open questions flag, writes back cited,
30	  and delivers an unmerged PR. Most passes correctly change nothing.
31	
32	## Rules
33	
34	| Rule | Enforces (≤5 words) | How |
35	|---|---|---|
36	| `product-wiki-layout` | skeleton exists (index + sink) | check, blocking |
37	| `product-wiki-page-sections` | pages carry the three sections | check, blocking |
38	| `product-wiki-growth-log` | log bullets dated, real dates | check, blocking |
39	| `product-wiki-sources` | source bullets carry their URL | check, blocking |
40	| `product-wiki-freshness` | stale wiki gets a nag | check, **advisory** |
41	| `product-wiki-isolation` | repo can't reference wiki space | check, blocking (fixed barrier) |
42	| sink is human-reviewed only | — | prose + worker must-never-do |
43	| cite / correct-with-note / no fabrication | — | prose + worker method |
44	| sample-data ≠ test fixtures | — | prose |
45	| unattended growth lands as unmerged PR | — | prose + worker delivery policy |

48	is time-driven (a repo goes stale with no change to its tree), and a

- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location and test-location exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). - single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo repo-tidy task hands you branches to assess).
